questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify what makes an exchange reciprocal
questions.stem: Two survey stations agree that each will host the other's field teams and share laboratory access. What makes their arrangement reciprocal rather than one-sided?

options.text: Each station gives and receives a comparable benefit, so a withdrawal by one would affect the other.
One station holds the senior role and the other accepts it, which makes the agreement legitimate.
options.misconception: treats hierarchy rather than mutual benefit as reciprocity

options.text: The arrangement was drafted by lawyers, which ensures that each side is treated identically.
options.misconception: believes legal drafting, not exchange, creates reciprocity

options.text: The agreement is renewable every five years, so the parties can always adjust the balance.
options.misconception: confuses a renewal mechanism with reciprocity between the parties

questions.explanation: Reciprocity depends on each party giving something the other values and being able to withhold it, so the relationship is mutual. Hierarchy, legal drafting, and renewal dates describe the form of the arrangement, not the mutual exchange.
questions.hint: Ask what each side would lose if the other walked away.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Read a treaty-count table and identify the binding share
questions.stem: Of 50 field stations that signed the shared sampling protocol, 38 accepted every clause, 9 accepted it subject to a stated reservation, and 3 signed without accepting any clause. How many accepted at least one binding clause without qualification?

options.text: 38, because only unqualified acceptance makes a clause binding.
options.misconception: counts only unqualified acceptance as binding participation

options.text: 50, because every signatory accepts the clauses it has not reserved against.
options.misconception: assumes silence means acceptance of reserved clauses

options.text: 47, counting the 38 unconditional acceptors and the 9 who reserved only some clauses.
12, because the reservations and the non-acceptors together cancel the protocol for the rest.
options.misconception: assumes one reservation invalidates the whole instrument

questions.explanation: A reservation narrows a party's acceptance but leaves the remaining clauses binding, so 38 plus 9 gives 47 parties bound by at least part of the protocol. Signatories that accepted nothing contribute nothing to that count.
questions.hint: A reservation carves clauses out, it does not void the rest.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain what makes a sanctions programme credible
questions.stem: A conservation body must design a scheme that pushes rogue fishing vessels out of a shared fishing ground. Explain what makes a sanctions programme credible rather than merely announced.

answer.exemplar: Credibility comes from the scheme's ability to impose real, foreseeable and proportionate costs on evasion, and from the fact that those costs are applied by people with the resources and information to identify violators. Rules must be clear about what counts as a breach, must be backed by inspection, monitoring and tracking systems that actually detect it, and must be applied to offenders of every nationality rather than to convenient targets. Announcements without detection capacity and even-handed enforcement will quickly be discounted, and once violators believe evasion is cheap the incentive to comply disappears.

questions.explanation: Credibility rests on detectable violations and costs that are actually imposed on offenders, applied even-handedly. Rules with no monitoring or no realistic consequence are read as cheap talk and change nobody's behaviour.
questions.hint: Ask whether evasion would actually be found and punished.

questions.topic: Reading a set of cost shares
questions.learningObjective: Compute a proportional share from site counts
questions.stem: A survey of 60 sampling sites costs 180,000 in total, and the cost is divided among the three regions that contain them in proportion to the number of sites each region holds. Region A holds 24 sites. What percentage of the total cost is assigned to Region A?
questions.explanation: Region A holds 24 of 60 sites, so its proportional share is 24 divided by 60, which is 0.4 or 40 percent of the cost. Assigning equal shares by region rather than by site count would misstate the allocation.
questions.hint: Divide the region's sites by the total sites, then scale by 100.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify a targeted rather than comprehensive enforcement design

stimulus.body: The protocol's enforcement annex lists specific measures: publication of the vessel's name and licence number, suspension of its permission to land catch at member ports, and seizure of its gear if it is found inside the protected zone. The annex states that no general measure, such as a ban on all fishing by flagged vessels, is authorised by this protocol.

questions.stem: Using only the annex above, which statement about the enforcement design is correct?

options.text: The annex authorises comprehensive measures against flagged vessels, since it names specific sanctions.
options.misconception: reads specific measures as a licence for blanket measures

options.text: The annex is deliberately targeted, listing defined measures and explicitly excluding general bans.
The annex is comprehensive, because naming three measures is enough to cover all misconduct.
options.misconception: treats a short list of measures as coverage of all misconduct

options.text: The annex creates a general obligation on all parties to act against any vessel in the zone.
options.misconception: infers a general duty from a list of specified measures

questions.explanation: The annex names three defined measures and says in terms that no general measure is authorised, so the design is targeted. A list of specific sanctions is the opposite of a comprehensive regime.
questions.hint: Notice what the annex says about general measures.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an unenforced warning fails to deter

stimulus.body: A reserve authority tells illegal hunters that their vehicles will be impounded if the vehicles are seen on the access road. Over the past two years the authority has impounded nothing, and it has never issued a published list of impoundments. Hunters continue to use the road, and local guides report that the warning is treated as a formality.

questions.stem: In the scenario above, why is the warning not functioning as a deterrent?

options.text: Because the warning is too vague, since hunters cannot tell which vehicles are covered.
options.misconception: blames wording rather than the absence of enforcement

options.text: Because hunters do not know the road is part of the reserve, so the warning never reached them.
options.misconception: invents an information gap the scenario does not mention

options.text: Because impounding vehicles is illegal under the reserve's charter, which forbids asset seizure.
options.misconception: invents a legal bar that the scenario never states

options.text: Because a threat that is never carried out carries no cost, so hunters reasonably ignore it.

questions.explanation: A threat influences behaviour only if it is believed and if violating it actually costs something. With no impoundments and no published record, hunters have good evidence that the warning is empty, so the expected penalty is zero.
questions.hint: Ask what a violator has actually paid so far.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify a principal-agent problem in a funding arrangement
questions.stem: A funder releases the final 30 percent of a survey's budget only if the research team files its raw data on schedule. Which analysis best describes this arrangement?

options.text: A principal-agent problem, because the funder cannot fully observe effort and uses staged payment to test it.
A collective action problem, because the team members must each agree to hand over data.
options.misconception: misreads an information problem as a cooperation problem

options.text: A free-riding problem, because the funder benefits from data the team has already produced.
options.misconception: treats staged payment as the enjoyment of others' output

options.text: A delegation problem, because the team has been given authority to spend the budget as it sees fit.
options.misconception: confuses discretionary spending authority with hidden effort

questions.explanation: The funder cannot observe how much effort the team puts in, so staged payment is a device for revealing it, which is the principal-agent pattern. Free-riding and collective action concern cooperation among many contributors, which is not what is at issue here.
questions.hint: Ask who cannot see what the other party is doing.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess whether a funding condition preserves the implementer's ownership
questions.stem: A team designed a monitoring protocol themselves, then agreed to fund it only if the results are published openly. Which is the strongest argument that the arrangement still gives the team ownership?

options.text: Because the funder can withdraw the money, the protocol cannot be directed by the funder.
options.misconception: reverses the direction of control, since money is the funder's lever

options.text: Because open publication is a condition, the team must keep working to retain the money.
options.misconception: treats external dependence as evidence of ownership

options.text: Because the team designed the protocol and the condition constrains only its use of funds.
Because the team can publish whatever it likes after the money is spent.
options.misconception: ignores that the funding condition still binds the team's conduct

questions.explanation: Ownership rests on the team having designed the work and on the condition limiting funding rather than dictating the science. Control over the purse creates leverage even when the design is the team's own, but it does not make the design someone else's.
questions.hint: Ask who determined the design and what the condition restricts.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify what supports the legitimacy of unelected rule-making
questions.stem: A technical panel of expert reviewers sets the method used to certify field equipment, and no member of it was elected. Which feature most supports the legitimacy of those rules?

options.text: The panel's members were appointed for life, which removes any possibility of political pressure.
options.misconception: treats life tenure as a guarantee of impartiality

options.text: The rules are published, open to comment, and applied with reasons that can be challenged.
The panel operates by consensus, so no single member can impose a rule on the others.
options.misconception: treats consensus as the same thing as public justification

options.text: The panel reports to the ministry, which gives it a clear line of political accountability.
options.misconception: mistakes ministerial oversight for public accountability

questions.explanation: Legitimacy for rules made by unelected officials comes from transparency, participation, and the ability to challenge decisions. Life tenure, internal consensus, and ministerial reporting address other concerns entirely.
questions.hint: Look for openness and a route of challenge.

questions.learningObjective: Compare the cost avoided by withdrawal at different times
questions.stem: Four stations leave a shared data archive at different times. One leaves after 1 year, one after 2 years, one after 3 years, and one after 4 years, and the annual archive cost is 5,000 per station-year. How much total cost does each station's exit avoid?

options.text: 5,000 for every station, because withdrawal happens at the same time each year.
options.misconception: assumes all departures occur at the same moment

options.text: 12,000 for every station, because the archive charges a flat exit fee.
options.misconception: invents a flat fee with no basis in the data

options.text: 60,000 for every station, because the archive cost is independent of how long a station stays.
options.misconception: treats the total archive cost as if it were the same per station

options.text: 5,000, 10,000, 15,000 and 20,000 respectively, from 1 to 4 years of avoided cost.

questions.explanation: Avoided cost is the annual charge multiplied by the years of membership, so 1 year avoids 5,000 while 4 years avoids 20,000. A flat or identical figure ignores that later withdrawal avoids more cost than earlier withdrawal.
questions.hint: Multiply the annual charge by each station's years of membership.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an unbalanced exchange is not reciprocal
questions.stem: Two laboratories exchange tissue samples and each receives twice the number of samples it provides. Explain why the exchange is not reciprocal, and what the imbalance does to the relationship.

answer.exemplar: Reciprocity requires that what each side gives is broadly matched by what it receives, so an exchange in which one laboratory contributes far more than it gets back does not run on mutual benefit. The imbalance tilts the arrangement: the laboratory supplying most of the material bears a disproportionate share of the cost, effort, and risk of handling samples it will never see results from, while the recipient gains access it has not paid for in equivalent terms. Over time this creates dependence, weakens the sense of joint ownership, and can end the exchange when the supplier concludes it is subsidising the other.

questions.explanation: Reciprocity needs roughly matched exchange, and twice the samples in one direction breaks that balance. The imbalance shifts cost and risk onto the supplier and weakens the mutual footing of the partnership.
questions.hint: Compare what each side gives with what each side gets.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the features that make an enforcement procedure credible

stimulus.body: The scheme sets out a three-stage process. First, a monitoring unit identifies suspected violations using vessel-tracking data and observer reports. Second, an independent panel reviews the evidence and decides whether a violation occurred. Third, a committee of member governments determines the sanction, and its decision and reasoning are published within thirty days.

questions.stem: According to the quoted procedure, what most clearly distinguishes this scheme from a list of threats?

options.text: The scheme names three stages, whereas most schemes name only one or two.
options.misconception: reads the number of stages as the substance of the design

options.text: The scheme includes a committee, whereas most schemes leave decisions to officials.
options.misconception: focuses on who decides without looking at evidence or reasons

options.text: The scheme separates detection, adjudication and decision, and publishes the reasoning.
The scheme publishes decisions within thirty days, which is faster than other schemes.
options.misconception: treats the publication deadline as the mark of credibility

questions.explanation: What makes a scheme credible is that detection, adjudication and sanction are separate steps, so no single body decides that guilt is proved and that punishment follows. Publishing the reasoning lets outsiders check the process, which matters more than the speed of publication.
questions.hint: Ask who investigates, who decides, and whether reasons are published.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Reading a set of cost shares
questions.learningObjective: Compute a regional charge from a per-site rate

stimulus.body: A ring of 12 wetland sites is monitored under one contract. The contract splits the cost so that each site pays 3,000 and each regional office pays a further 2,000 per site in its region. Four regions are involved, with 5, 3, 2 and 2 sites respectively.

questions.stem: In the scenario above, how much does the region holding three sites pay for its regional contribution?

options.text: 6,000, which is 2,000 multiplied by the three sites in that region.
9,000, which is 3,000 for each site plus the regional charge for three sites.
options.misconception: adds the per-site fee into a question about the regional charge

options.text: 24,000, which is the site's share of the whole ring spread across three sites.
options.misconception: divides the whole contract cost instead of the regional charge

options.text: 4,000, because the regional charge is divided equally among the region's sites.
options.misconception: assumes the regional charge is split equally among the region's sites

questions.explanation: The regional contribution is 2,000 per site, so a region with three sites owes 6,000. Adding the 3,000 site fee answers a different question, and dividing the whole contract cost by region is not how the contract allocates.
questions.hint: Multiply the regional rate by the number of sites it covers.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the argument that a targeted scheme is too weak
questions.stem: A reviewer argues that because the enforcement annex lists only three sanctions, the scheme is too weak to deter evasion. Which evaluation of the argument is sound?

options.text: The argument is correct, because deterrence always requires more than three possible penalties.
options.misconception: assumes deterrence depends on the number of listed penalties

options.text: The argument is correct, because targeted measures fail against vessels from states that are not members.
options.misconception: invents a non-member enforcement gap the annex does not describe

options.text: The argument is weak, because comprehensive bans are always more effective than targeted ones.
options.misconception: presupposes that comprehensive measures are always superior

options.text: The argument is weak, because credible detection and even-handed application matter more than the number of measures.

questions.explanation: Deterrence rests on violators expecting to be detected and sanctioned, not on the length of the penalty list, so the argument misidentifies what matters. Whether comprehensive bans would work better is not established by the annex either.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Infer credibility from a record of enforcement
questions.stem: An authority threatens to close a fishery for six months if catch limits are exceeded. In the last three years it has imposed that closure twice. What does that record imply about the threat's credibility?

options.text: It is credible, because a six-month closure is a severe penalty.
options.misconception: judges credibility by severity alone rather than by delivery

options.text: It is credible, because the penalty has actually been applied twice in three years.
It is not credible, because two closures in three years show the threat is applied too often.
options.misconception: mistakes repeated application for evidence of weakness

options.text: It is not credible, because three years is too short a period to judge any record.
options.misconception: dismisses an available record for being short rather than testing it

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Select a measure that addresses an unobservable effort problem
questions.stem: A funder cannot observe how many hours a field team actually logs, but it can inspect completed protocols and data quality. Which measure best addresses the funder's problem?

options.text: Paying the whole budget upfront, which removes the temptation to misreport.
options.misconception: assumes removing payment risk removes the need for observation

options.text: Requiring the team to recruit its own staff, which aligns their incentives with the funder's.
options.misconception: confuses recruitment with a measurable performance signal

options.text: Releasing funds in stages against verified deliverables, which ties money to observable performance.
Publishing the team's funding agreement, which makes any misreporting visible to rivals.
options.misconception: relies on external reputation rather than the funder's own monitoring

questions.explanation: The funder's difficulty is that effort is partly unobservable, and staged payment against checkable deliverables creates an observable signal without needing to watch the team. Upfront payment removes the leverage, and reputation is too slow and noisy to serve as the primary check.
questions.hint: Link the money the funder controls to something it can verify.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how unelected rule-making can still be legitimate
questions.stem: An expert body sets the criteria that decide which laboratories may publish monitoring results used in a national assessment. Explain how its rules can be legitimate even though nobody voted for its members.

answer.exemplar: Legitimacy here does not come from election but from the procedure around the rules. The criteria must be published before they are applied, comments must be invited from affected laboratories, the reasoning for each decision must be recorded and open to challenge by an appeal or review body, and the terms of office must be fixed and renewable so that members cannot stay indefinitely without scrutiny. Each of these gives the rule-making body reasons to show its work and a route for others to contest its output. That is what allows rules set by experts to be accepted without giving the experts any electoral mandate.

questions.explanation: Legitimacy comes from publishing the criteria, inviting comment, giving reasons and allowing challenge, plus fixed renewable terms for members. Elections are one route to legitimacy, not the only one.
questions.hint: Think about procedure around the rules, not who cast votes.

questions.learningObjective: Derive a conclusion about reciprocity from a quoted memorandum

options.text: Reciprocity exists because contributions are matched and each side can withhold the same benefit.

options.misconception: ignores the effect of the recorded reservation

questions.learningObjective: Select the change that most improves a scheme's credibility

questions.learningObjective: Interpret enforcement outcomes for a pattern of warnings

options.misconception: confuses detection with compliance and ignores the outcomes

options.misconception: assumes detection counts as proof of a high breach rate

options.text: The monitoring regime is unnecessary, since violators appear to correct themselves after warnings.
options.misconception: reads warnings as effective correction without evidence

questions.explanation: Every detected breach produced a warning and no penalty, so violators learn that being seen costs nothing, and the threat stops deterring. The low detection count reflects monitoring reach rather than compliance.
questions.hint: Ask what a detected violator learned from the response.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a funding condition is not merely paperwork
questions.stem: A funder attaches a condition to a grant: the final payment is released only if the data meet a published quality threshold. Explain why this is a conditionality problem rather than simply a grant with paperwork.

answer.exemplar: The problem is that the funder cannot see the quality of the work while it is being done; what is observable is the deliverable at the point where payment is decided. The condition therefore creates a benchmark the team is likely to anticipate and shape its work towards, which is exactly what makes it a conditionality problem rather than administrative paperwork: the design of the condition, its timing, and what counts as meeting it all shape the research that is actually done. Better monitoring that could observe effort directly, and reporting that the funder could verify rather than a threshold chosen in advance, would weaken that distortion.

questions.explanation: Conditionality uses payment to steer work whose quality cannot be observed in progress, and the team will shape its methods to meet the condition. Where the funder can observe effort directly, plain monitoring is the better instrument.
questions.hint: Think about what the team does differently because of the condition.

questions.explanation: External funders provide 250,000 of the 400,000 budget, and that share, 62.5 percent, is the portion released subject to the condition. Attaching the condition to the whole budget would overstate the funding that is actually at stake.
questions.hint: Divide the conditioned funding by the total budget, then scale by 100.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the procedural feature that supports legitimacy

stimulus.body: The certification rule is issued in draft form at least sixty days before it takes effect, with a written comment period open to any laboratory. The final text records the comments received and the panel's response to each, and states the date on which the next review of the rule will be held.

questions.stem: Using only the quoted text, which feature most directly supports the legitimacy of the rule?

options.text: The rule is issued in draft form, so laboratories can prepare for it.
options.misconception: reads advance notice, which helps preparation, as a legitimacy feature

options.text: The rule states the date of the next review, so it will not last forever.
options.misconception: treats a review date as evidence of procedural fairness

options.text: Comment is invited and the panel's responses are recorded, so the rule's basis is inspectable.
The rule applies to laboratories generally, so it treats everyone equally.
options.misconception: mistakes general application for procedural legitimacy

questions.explanation: Legitimacy for unelected rule-makers comes from participation and reasons, and the quoted text supplies both by recording comments and the response to them. Advance notice and general application help with administration and coverage, not with justification.
questions.hint: Ask whether affected parties could affect the text.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess the effect of late withdrawal on remaining members

stimulus.body: The shared archive lets stations leave at any time but prices the exit by how much shared infrastructure each station has used. A station that leaves early releases the assets but still owes a share of the depreciation already incurred, while a station that leaves after full use of its allotment has nothing further to owe beyond its unused years.

questions.stem: In the scenario above, what is the effect on the remaining stations of one station leaving late rather than early?

options.text: They lose the departing station's contributions but gain access to the assets it releases.
options.misconception: misses the cost of depreciation the departing station still owes

options.text: They are little affected, since a late departure avoids the unused-year charges.
They must absorb the departing station's unused years because those charges are prepaid.
options.misconception: inverts who bears the unused-year charges on a late departure

options.text: They gain nothing, because released assets cannot be redistributed among the members.
options.misconception: assumes released assets are unusable by the remaining stations

questions.explanation: A late departure means the station has used its full allotment, so it owes nothing beyond charges it has already paid and the remaining stations lose little. An early departure leaves unused-year charges and unrecovered depreciation for others to absorb.
questions.hint: Ask who is left holding the departing station's unused capacity.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess the effect of an exit clause on reciprocity
questions.stem: One station proposes that if the other pulls out of the shared programme, the first may keep the data and equipment it has already received. What is the most likely effect of this clause?

options.text: It strengthens reciprocity, because it protects the party that has already given the most.
options.misconception: treats protection of the giver as a reciprocity improvement

options.text: It has no effect, because data and equipment are never returnable under any agreement.
options.misconception: asserts non-returnability that the clause itself contradicts

options.text: It discourages all cooperation, because no station would share anything with any other.
options.misconception: generalises from one clause to the end of all cooperation

options.text: It weakens reciprocity, because the party that exits can keep benefits while others lose theirs.

questions.explanation: Reciprocity depends on benefits flowing in both directions and on losses being mutual, and a clause that lets one side exit while keeping what it received breaks that symmetry. It does not end cooperation generally, but it gives one side a reason to hold back later.
questions.hint: Ask who keeps what when the arrangement ends.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Count the parties bound by a reserved article
questions.stem: A treaty binds 30 parties. Eleven entered reservations, three withdrew theirs, and two of the remaining reservists acceded to the article before it entered into force. How many parties are bound by that article?

options.text: 24, because 30 parties minus the 6 still maintaining reservations leaves 24 bound.
27, because only the parties that never entered a reservation are excluded.
options.misconception: ignores withdrawn and lapsed reservations in the count

options.text: 19, because 30 parties minus 11 reservations leaves 19 bound to the article.
options.misconception: fails to add back the withdrawn and lapsed reservations

options.text: 30, because a reservation suspends a dispute without removing any party's obligations.
options.misconception: treats a reservation as a dispute procedure rather than an exception

questions.explanation: Eleven reservations less three withdrawals and two lapses leaves six in force, so 30 minus 6 gives 24 parties bound by the article. Counting withdrawn or lapsed reservations as live, or ignoring reservations entirely, changes the answer.
questions.hint: Work out how many reservations still stand, then subtract.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the gap left by a published enforcement scheme
questions.stem: A scheme publishes the criteria for a violation, names the penalty for it, and names the body that applies it. Which feature does that combination still leave unclear?

options.text: Which conduct counts as a violation, since the criteria are published.
options.misconception: repeats a settled feature as if it were the gap

options.text: Who applies the penalty, since the applying body is named.
options.misconception: repeats a settled feature as if it were the gap

options.text: How violations are detected and verified before any penalty is applied.
How serious the offence is, since the penalty is set out in the scheme.
options.misconception: treats the penalty scale as evidence that seriousness is clear

questions.explanation: Publishing criteria and naming a penalty tell you what breaks the rule and what follows, but not how a breach is established in practice. Without a detection and verification step, the scheme cannot operate consistently.
questions.hint: Ask what happens between the conduct and the penalty.

questions.stem: Three regional offices share a survey budget of 96,000 in proportion to the 5, 3 and 4 field teams they host. What is the allocation to the office hosting 4 teams?

options.text: 32,000, because the budget is divided equally among the three offices.
options.misconception: splits the budget equally rather than by the number of teams

options.text: 32,000, because 4 of the 12 teams times 96,000 gives 32,000.
24,000, because 4 of the 12 teams times 72,000 gives 24,000.
options.misconception: uses a budget figure that the problem does not state

options.text: 40,000, because the office with the most teams is charged above the stated rate.
options.misconception: invents a surcharge for the largest office

questions.explanation: With 12 teams in total, the office hosting 4 holds one third of the survey, and one third of 96,000 is 32,000. Equal splitting between offices or a surcharge on the largest would contradict the stated allocation rule.
questions.hint: Find the office's fraction of teams, then apply it to the budget.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Weigh the case for and against a targeted enforcement design
questions.stem: An enforcement annex authorises specific measures against vessels that breach a reserve rule and expressly forbids general measures. Explain the case for and against that targeted design.

answer.exemplar: The case for targeting is that defined measures attached to identified breaches are easier to apply consistently, easier to explain to operators, and less likely to punish conduct that is innocent or ambiguous. The case against is that the narrower the list, the more room an operator has to find a breach that is not covered, and a scheme with no general reserve also has no way to respond to a serious or novel violation. A workable compromise keeps the specific measures as the ordinary route and provides a defined general power, triggered by clear criteria, for cases the list does not reach, so that the gap is closed by procedure rather than by blanket discretion.

questions.explanation: Targeting helps consistent application and clearer expectations, but leaves gaps that a determined evader can exploit. A defined general power for uncovered cases closes the gap without granting unlimited discretion.
questions.hint: Weigh consistency against the gaps a short list leaves.

questions.explanation: All 5 detected breaches attracted the doubled fee, so the penalty rate is 5 out of 5, which is 100 percent. Using the 40 licences issued as the denominator would answer a different question about detection rather than enforcement.
questions.hint: Divide penalties imposed by breaches detected.

questions.topic: Reading a set of cost shares
questions.learningObjective: Read a withdrawal clause about liability for fixed costs

stimulus.body: The cost note states that each member shall bear one quarter of the fixed costs of the network, that variable costs shall be allocated in proportion to the number of nights each member occupies a monitoring station, and that any member that withdraws during a year shall remain liable for its share of fixed costs incurred up to the date of withdrawal.

questions.stem: According to the note, what happens to a member's liability for fixed costs if it withdraws mid-year?

options.text: It stays liable for the fixed costs it caused up to the date it withdrew.
It ends entirely at withdrawal, because future fixed costs are not its responsibility.
options.misconception: misreads the clause as cutting off liability at the withdrawal date

options.text: It doubles, because withdrawal triggers an additional penalty under the note.
options.misconception: invents a penalty that the note does not mention

options.text: It continues for the whole year, because the note sets no date for ending liability.
options.misconception: ignores the stated cut-off at the date of withdrawal

questions.explanation: The note limits liability to fixed costs incurred up to the withdrawal date, so a member leaving mid-year remains responsible for the share it caused before leaving. Liability does not end entirely, and nothing in the note creates a penalty or extends liability past that date.
questions.hint: Read the clause on withdrawal and fixed costs closely.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose the weakness of an observable but gameable condition

stimulus.body: A funder releases 70 percent of a grant at the start of the year and the remaining 30 percent after an inspection of the team's submitted data. The inspection can only check that the required fields were completed and the protocol was followed; it cannot evaluate whether the fieldwork was done with care. Two teams have taken shortcuts to reach the completion thresholds, and both received the second payment.

questions.stem: In the scenario above, what does the case show about the conditionality arrangement?

options.text: The inspection is too strict, because it checks completion rather than the value of the data.
options.misconception: blames the rigour of the check instead of what it can observe

options.text: The condition can be satisfied superficially, because the observable measure is easy to meet.
The teams were right to take shortcuts, because the funder set an unrealistic standard.
options.misconception: treats weak monitoring as an unreasonable standard

options.text: Staged payment is the wrong instrument, because the teams had already spent the first 70 percent.
options.misconception: assumes staged payment fails where funds are already committed

questions.explanation: The condition ties money to a measure that is easy to satisfy superficially, so teams can game it while the funder remains unable to observe care. This is a weakness of the monitoring measure, not of the team's compliance in the formal sense.
questions.hint: Ask what the inspection can see and what it cannot.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the effect of externally framed research questions
questions.stem: A funder offers 40 percent of a survey's cost, but only if the survey answers questions set by the funder. Which evaluation best describes the effect on the survey's ownership?

options.text: Ownership is unaffected, because funding rarely affects who directs research.
options.misconception: denies that money shapes research priorities

options.text: Ownership increases, because the funder's questions guarantee the work will be useful.
options.misconception: treats external framing as a gain in ownership

options.text: Ownership is unaffected, because the survey team still carries out the fieldwork.
options.misconception: confuses who executes the work with who shapes it

options.text: Ownership is diluted, because the questions the work must answer are set outside the team.

questions.explanation: Ownership depends on whose questions the work answers, and framing them externally dilutes the team's claim to direct the research even if the team does the fieldwork and publishes the results. External money alone does not create ownership, and it does not automatically destroy it either.
questions.hint: Ask who set the questions the survey answers.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Weigh procedural openness against composition imbalance
questions.stem: An expert body sets 6 certification criteria and answers 14 public objections in a comment period. Only 2 of its 9 members are drawn from the laboratories the criteria affect. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The criteria are illegitimate, because 7 of 9 members come from outside the affected sector.
options.misconception: treats sector imbalance as the sole test of legitimacy

options.text: The criteria are legitimate, because answering objections demonstrates openness.
options.misconception: ignores the composition imbalance as relevant evidence

options.text: Openness is demonstrated, but the imbalance may still weaken the appearance of impartiality.
The criteria are illegitimate, because any imbalance in composition defeats the process.
options.misconception: makes composition imbalance automatically fatal to legitimacy

questions.explanation: Answering objections shows procedural openness, which is one real support for legitimacy, while the composition imbalance leaves a reasonable concern that the body will not be seen as neutral. Neither factor settles the question alone.

options.text: The length of membership, because refunds scale with the years of contributions made.
The size of each station's field team, because refunds scale with staff numbers.
options.misconception: invents a staffing rule that the refund formula does not contain

options.text: The agreement's total budget, because refunds are proportional to the whole archive.
options.misconception: ties the refund to the overall budget rather than to contributions

options.text: Nothing, because a shared archive never refunds a departing member.
options.misconception: denies the existence of any refund rule

questions.explanation: Where a refund formula scales with contributions over time, later departure returns more, because more contributions have been made. Staff numbers, the total budget, or the absence of refunds are not what the formula turns on.

questions.learningObjective: Assess the balance of an exchange across two seasons

options.misconception: ignores that receipts rose to match supply

options.text: The exchange became less balanced, because X's net contribution fell from 30 to 0 field-days.
options.misconception: treats a smaller surplus as a worse imbalance

options.misconception: judges balance by volume growth rather than by surplus

options.text: The exchange became balanced, because X's surplus of 30 field-days disappeared.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why comprehensive measures suit a mixed population poorly
questions.stem: A reserve authority must reduce illegal trawling without closing the whole fishery to everyone. Explain why a scheme built only on comprehensive measures would be a poor choice here.

answer.exemplar: A comprehensive measure, such as a blanket ban on all fishing in the zone, would impose the full cost of a few offenders on every legitimate operator, including those who have never breached anything. Because the zone supports the livelihood of many licensed fishers, the loss of access would be widely felt and politically hard to sustain, and it would drive effort into adjacent waters rather than reducing it. A targeted scheme, in which defined measures attach to identified breaches and are applied to offenders of every nationality, concentrates the cost where the wrongdoing is, protects the base of compliant operators, and gives monitoring teams a clear, checkable objective.

questions.explanation: Comprehensive measures punish everyone for the conduct of a few, which is inefficient and politically fragile, and they divert effort elsewhere. Targeted measures concentrate cost on offenders while leaving compliant operators alone.
questions.hint: Ask who bears the cost of a blanket ban.

questions.hint: Remove the reservists, divide by the total, then scale by 100.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify what makes an enforcement threat credible

stimulus.body: The enforcement note states that inspections of the protected zone are carried out on a published monthly schedule by named officers, that each inspection produces a signed record of what was found, and that a summary of every inspection is posted for the public each quarter. It further states that where a breach is confirmed, the vessel is barred from the zone for a minimum of twelve months.

questions.stem: Based on the note, which feature most supports the credibility of the enforcement threat?

options.text: The note sets a twelve-month minimum ban, so the threat is severe enough to deter.
options.misconception: judges credibility by severity instead of by expected detection

options.text: The note publishes a schedule, records and results, so violations can be found and checked.
The note names the inspecting officers, so violators can be held personally responsible.
options.misconception: mistakes named officers for public verification of enforcement

options.text: The note posts quarterly summaries, which shows the authority is transparent about its work.
options.misconception: separates transparency from the detection capacity the threat needs

questions.explanation: Credibility rests on violators expecting to be found and sanctioned, and the note supplies the ingredients: a routine schedule, signed records, published results, and a defined consequence. Severity and transparency help, but neither produces detection on its own.
questions.hint: Ask whether a violator could reasonably expect to be caught.

questions.learningObjective: Judge how much a condition actually constrains conduct

stimulus.body: A field station accepts 30 percent of a survey's cost from a funder on condition that the funder approves the final report before publication. options.misconception: overstates a routine approval as a substantive veto

options.text: It increases the station's ownership, because external review improves the quality of the report.
options.misconception: mistakes external review for a gain in ownership

options.text: It is largely formal, because the funder approves quickly and never alters the analysis.
It transfers ownership to the funder, because the funder's name appears on the report.
options.misconception: treats acknowledgment of funding as a transfer of ownership

questions.explanation: A condition changes behaviour only through the discretion it gives the party imposing it, and a funder that approves in days and never touches the analysis leaves the station's intellectual control intact. A veto in principle matters only if it is used.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why published inspection records strengthen a warning
questions.stem: A reserve authority issues warnings to boats that enter a closure zone. Explain why warnings alone are likely to be less effective than warnings backed by published inspection records.

answer.exemplar: Warnings work only to the extent that the person warned believes the rule is real and that violating it carries a cost. A warning with no record of any action suggests the rule is decorative, and once operators form that belief the warning adds nothing, however stern its wording. Published inspection records, names of inspecting officers, and results for every patrol give operators evidence that detection is routine and that some consequence follows detection, so the warning becomes credible information about what will actually happen. That evidence converts an announcement into a probability the operator can reasonably price into its decision to enter the zone.

questions.explanation: A warning signals a rule but reveals nothing about its enforcement, while published inspection records show that detection is routine and consequences follow. Operators price that evidence into their decisions, so credibility comes from demonstrated enforcement rather than from wording.
questions.hint: Ask what a record of enforcement tells an operator.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the inspection effort needed for targeted measures
questions.stem: A reserve zone admits 200 licensed vessels, of which 14 were caught breaching the closure rule. An enforcement annex authorises three targeted measures, and the authority wants to apply all three to every detected breach. If each measure requires one inspector-day, how many inspector-days are needed?
questions.explanation: Fourteen breaches each requiring three measures at one inspector-day apiece needs 42 inspector-days. Applying the measures to all 200 licensed vessels would need 600 inspector-days, which is not what the scheme authorises.
questions.hint: Multiply the number of breaches by the measures applied to each.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Separate what a condition ties money to from what it reserves

stimulus.body: The grant agreement states that the funder's final 25 percent of costs is payable when the survey has deposited all primary data in the designated public repository and has published a methods paper describing the sampling design. The agreement also states that the survey team retains sole responsibility for the sampling design, for the choice of sites, and for the interpretation of results.

questions.stem: Based on the agreement, what does the condition do and leave alone?

options.text: It leaves the sampling design to the funder, since deposit requirements are set centrally.
options.misconception: contradicts the clause reserving design to the team

options.text: It removes the team's ownership of interpretation, because the methods paper must be published.
options.misconception: treats publication of methods as transferring interpretation rights

options.text: It has no effect on ownership, because depositing data is an administrative formality.
options.misconception: dismisses a condition that changes how the team works

options.text: It attaches money to data deposit and methods publication while leaving design and interpretation with the team.

questions.explanation: The condition ties the final payment to verifiable outputs, which is a real constraint on the team's conduct, but the agreement explicitly reserves design, site choice and interpretation to the team. The condition targets outputs rather than decisions.
questions.hint: Separate what the money is tied to from what the team decides.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess the accountability of an unelected standards panel

stimulus.body: A standards panel of 9 unelected experts issues rules that determine which monitoring methods count as acceptable evidence. Its meetings are open, its minutes are published within a week, and any party may request a review of a decision. Last year it rejected an appeal from a laboratory on a point of procedure, and the published minutes do not record the reasons for that rejection.

questions.stem: In the scenario above, which evaluation of the panel's accountability is sound?

options.text: Procedural openness is real, but the failure to record reasons weakens reviewability.
The panel is fully accountable, because an appeal route exists even if it rarely succeeds.
options.misconception: treats the existence of an appeal route as proof of accountability

options.text: The panel is unaccountable, because its members were never elected by anyone.
options.misconception: requires election as the only route to accountability

options.text: The panel is unaccountable, because published minutes without reasons are just publicity.
options.misconception: conflates unpublished reasoning with an absence of any disclosure

questions.explanation: Open meetings, prompt minutes and an appeal route are genuine accountability features, so the panel is not unaccountable for want of any procedure. The specific failure here is that reasons for the rejection are missing, which is exactly what a review needs.
questions.hint: Ask what a reviewer would still be missing.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Reading a set of cost shares
questions.learningObjective: Derive proportional shares from stated site counts
questions.stem: One survey covers 3 regions with 4, 5 and 7 sites, and the budget is split strictly by site count. Which statement follows from that rule?

options.text: The region with 5 sites receives 31.25 percent of the budget and the region with 7 sites receives 43.75 percent.
Each region receives the same amount, because all three regions are covered by one survey.
options.misconception: assumes one survey means one share for each region

options.text: The region with 4 sites receives more per site, because fewer sites share a fixed overhead.
options.misconception: invents a weighting that the stated rule excludes

options.text: The budget cannot be split, because the rule depends on a figure not given in the brief.
options.misconception: misses that the site counts are sufficient to apply the rule

questions.explanation: With 16 sites in total, 5 sites is 31.25 percent and 7 sites is 43.75 percent, which follows directly from the proportional rule. A per-site adjustment contradicts the rule as stated, and the site counts are all that is needed.
questions.hint: Divide each region's sites by the total of 16.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compute the net cost avoided by an early exit
questions.stem: A network charges 2,000 a year per member and a withdrawal fee of 10,000, but refunds the unused share of each annual payment if a member leaves early. If a member leaves after two years of a three-year term, what is the net cost it avoids by leaving rather than completing the term?

options.text: 10,000, because the withdrawal fee is the only amount the departing member avoids.
options.misconception: ignores the refunded annual payment in the net cost

options.text: 2,000, because only the final annual payment is at stake for a two-year member.
options.misconception: counts one year instead of the year remaining

options.text: 8,000, because the 2,000 final payment is refunded but the 10,000 fee is still paid.
4,000, because the departing member keeps half the unused annual payment.
options.misconception: invents a partial refund rule that the scheme does not contain

questions.explanation: The third annual payment of 2,000 is refunded on early departure but the 10,000 withdrawal fee is still payable, so the net amount saved is 8,000. Treating the fee as saved, or counting only part of the unused year, misstates the arithmetic.
questions.hint: Subtract what is refunded from what would otherwise be paid.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the feature that makes an exchange reciprocal
questions.stem: Two stations swap a fixed number of field-days each season under a memorandum. Which single feature makes the arrangement reciprocal rather than a one-way gift?

options.text: Each station's contribution depends on receiving the other's, so neither can keep what it takes without giving.
Each station sends more field-days than it receives, so the larger party subsidises the other.
options.misconception: treats unequal exchange as the test of reciprocity

options.text: Each station's contribution is fixed in advance, so neither can increase its share unilaterally.
options.misconception: treats a fixed quota as the mark of reciprocity

options.text: Each station's contribution is recorded and published, so the exchange is visible to outsiders.
options.misconception: mistakes transparency for mutuality of benefit

questions.explanation: Reciprocity is about contingency: each side's benefit depends on the other's contribution, so benefits and losses are mutual. Fixed quotas, unequal volumes, and publication concern predictability, imbalance and transparency rather than reciprocity itself.
questions.hint: Ask whether each side's gain depends on the other.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Track reservations through withdrawals and accessions
questions.stem: Of 80 members, 24 lodged reservations, 9 withdrew them, and 5 of the remaining 15 were acceded to the article before entry into force. How many members are not bound by the article?

options.text: 6, because 15 remaining reservations minus 9 withdrawals leaves 6 members unbound.
options.misconception: fails to remove the 5 that acceded to the article

options.text: 10, because 15 reservations remain after withdrawals and 5 of those acceded.
24, because the original number of reservations is what counts at the end.
options.misconception: ignores withdrawals and accessions to the reserved article

options.text: 15, because the withdrawals only delay the reservations rather than ending them.
options.misconception: treats withdrawal of a reservation as a mere suspension

questions.explanation: Twenty-four reservations less nine withdrawals leaves 15, and 5 of those acceded to the article, so 10 members remain unbound by it. Counting the original filings, or treating a withdrawal as a delay, contradicts the sequence.
questions.hint: Track the reservations through withdrawals and accessions.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how staged payment changes research behaviour
questions.stem: A funder pays a research group in two instalments, the second only once the group's interim findings are delivered. Explain how this arrangement can change what the group does, even where nobody has broken any rule.

answer.exemplar: The arrangement changes behaviour through anticipation rather than through enforcement. Because the second instalment depends on an interim output the funder can check, the group has an incentive to produce a deliverable that looks complete and presentable at the point of review, and to shape its methods towards what the funder will recognise as progress. Those incentives are not dishonest, but they can pull the work towards visible milestones and away from the messier questions the group originally wanted to answer. It follows that a good conditionality design fixes the review point and the criteria in advance, so that the incentive to demonstrate progress does not quietly replace the incentive to do the research well.

questions.explanation: Staged payment makes the group's progress at the review point consequential, so it shapes the work toward checkable deliverables even without any breach. Fixing criteria and timing in advance limits that distortion.
questions.hint: Ask what the group does differently before anyone checks.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compute the drafting time needed for public responses
questions.stem: An expert panel issues 9 certification criteria and receives 36 written objections. If the panel intends to publish a response to each objection and allows 6 minutes per response, how many minutes of drafting time does that require?
questions.explanation: Thirty-six responses at 6 minutes each require 216 minutes of drafting time. Treating the response as a single consolidated statement would give a far smaller figure, and the per-response rate is what the question specifies.
questions.hint: Multiply the number of objections by the minutes each takes.
